text:
Aisha: Heads-up — after the Terraform rename of the serviceAccount we started seeing app pods fail to mount secrets. Not a crashloop, just config files missing from /etc/config. Anyone seen this pattern with EKS + IRSA?

Ben: Hm, do you mean k8s secret volumes are empty or the projected serviceAccount token volume is missing?

Aisha: k8s secret volumes empty. The CSI secrets driver isn't erroring, mounts exist but files are zero bytes. Pods used to be fine before we swapped to aws_iam_service_account in TF module.

Carlos: Could be a timing/owner mismatch — if the SA name changed, the SecretProviderClass or some controller referencing the old SA might not have permissions. Do you have the SA YAML and the pod volume snippet?

Aisha: Here's the SA we now create via TF (redacted):
```yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: ServiceAccount
metadata:
  name: myapp-svc
  namespace: staging
  annotations:
    eks.amazonaws.com/role-arn: arn:aws:iam::123456789012:role/redwood-myapp-role
```
And pod volume (helm template):
```yaml
volumes:
  - name: app-config
    secret:
      secretName: myapp-config
containers:
  - name: app
    volumeMounts:
      - name: app-config
        mountPath: /etc/config
        readOnly: true
```

Ben: Looks normal. Quick checks: 1) kubectl get secret myapp-config -n staging -o yaml 2) kubectl describe pod <pod> -n staging 3) check CSI driver logs on the node. Maybe the secret got recreated with no data.

Carlos: Also verify the SA's automountServiceAccountToken setting — some controllers use the token to fetch secrets when mounting (e.g., external-secrets). If TF module defaulted to automount=false you could see this.

Aisha: Good call — running the checks now. Ran `kubectl get secret myapp-config -n staging -o yaml` and it's populated. Pod describe shows volume mounted but container sees zero-byte files. CSI logs show permission denied when trying to write to the mount inside the pod: `write /etc/config/app.yaml: permission denied`

Ben: That suggests the file owner/permissions on the mount are wrong. What user is the container running as? Any securityContext changes in the new chart?

Aisha: Container runs as uid 1002. Previously chart had `securityContext: fsGroup: 1002` but I realize we changed chart values in the same PR — I removed a deprecated fsGroup setting because I thought it was redundant with PodSecurityContext. Possibly I removed it incorrectly.

Carlos: Bingo. If fsGroup was removed, the mounted secret files might be owned by root and not writable, and some CSI drivers create files with restrictive perms. Add back podSecurityContext.fsGroup or containerSecurityContext.runAsUser/runAsGroup to match.

Aisha: Reapplying helm with fsGroup: 1002 fixed it on one staging pod. Files now present and readable. Thanks! :relieved:

DevOps Bot: deploy-myapp staging/slot-1 v1.3.8 rolled out — 1/3 pods restarted (manual rollback available). :rocket:

Ben: Nice find. Can you update the TF/helm PR with note about fsGroup and why we needed it? Might prevent future confusion if SA changes again.

Aisha: Yep — I'll add a comment and put a test that ensures mounted files are readable by the app user in helm chart tests.

Carlos: Also add a quick checklist item: when migrating to aws_iam_service_account, confirm automountServiceAccountToken and fsGroup semantics. Saved us a good debugging cycle.

Aisha: Will do. Thanks everyone! :thumbsup:
